name: Lost in the mall technique
aliases: Lost in a shopping mall study
statement: Given a fabricated childhood event vouched for by a relative and asked about it twice, a substantial minority of adults report remembering it.
meaning: This is a procedure rather than a bias, and the site's entry on false memory covers the wider literature it belongs to. A relative supplies three events from the participant's childhood that did happen, and confirms that a fourth, being lost in a shopping centre at about the age of five, did not. All four are written up as short narratives and posted to the participant, who is asked to remember each one. Two interviews follow. What gets counted at the end is a coder's judgement about a transcript, which is where most of the argument about this paradigm now sits. The design has a second feature that carries the whole result: the false event is ordinary, it is plausible for the person it is given to, and it arrives with a family member's authority behind it.

origin.who: Elizabeth F. Loftus and Jacqueline E. Pickrell
origin.note: The published study is 1995, and the procedure is older. Loftus and Pickrell credit an earlier case, reported as Loftus and Coan, in which a 14-year-old called Chris was fed a false memory of being lost at the University City mall in Spokane by his older brother. Crook and Dean's abstract dates the paradigm to five pilot experiments in 1991, involving three children and two adults. It gives 10 August 1992 as the date the University of Washington's Human Subjects Committee approved the study, and says the preliminary results from the five pilot subjects were announced four days later. James Coan, the student who ran the family pilot, published his own account in Ethics and Behavior in 1997.

evidence: Loftus and Pickrell ran 24 people, 3 men and 21 women, aged 18 to 53. Each was mailed a five-page booklet holding four one-paragraph stories from their childhood, three true and one crafted by the researchers. The relative was asked to name where the family shopped when the participant was about five, which stores would have drawn the child's interest, and to confirm the participant had never been lost in a mall. The false narrative was assembled from five fixed elements: lost for an extended period, crying, lost in a mall or large department store at about the age of five, found and helped by an elderly woman, and reunited with the family. Participants were interviewed twice, one to two weeks apart. They remembered something about 49 of the 72 true events, 68%. Seven of the 24 wrote something about the mall event in the booklet. At the first interview one of the seven decided she did not remember it, leaving 6 of 24, or 25%, claiming full or partial memory, and the figure held at the second interview. The false reports were thinner than the true ones, with a mean of 49.9 words against 138.0. At debriefing 19 of the 24 picked the mall event as the fabricated one. The paper's own summary of what it had shown is narrow: Loftus and Pickrell wrote that they made no claims about the percentage of people who might be misled this way. In the earlier family case, Chris rated his three true memories 1, 10 and 5 for clarity on an 11-point scale and the mall memory 8, and when told which event was false he had trouble believing it.

replication.headline: A preregistered repeat with five times the sample coded 35% of participants as having a false memory, against 25% in 1995, and a reanalysis of those same transcripts by stricter rules put the figure at 4%.
replication.detail: Murphy and nine colleagues in Cork and Dublin re-ran the protocol on 123 participants with a preregistered analysis plan, and coded 35% as reporting a false memory of being lost. Their abstract adds that mock jurors were also likely to believe the fabricated event had happened. The same team's debriefing paper reports the self-report side of that sample: 17 participants, 13.8%, said at the end of the second interview that they remembered the event, and a further 64, 52%, said they believed it had happened. So two-thirds of the sample took the suggestion in some form, and a quarter as many said they remembered it as the coders said did. Scoboria and six co-authors had already shown how much the scoring matters. They built a seven-part coding scheme, covering acceptance of the suggestion, elaboration beyond it, imagery, coherence, emotion, memory statements and not rejecting the suggestion, and applied it to transcripts from eight published implantation studies, N = 423. It classified 30.4% of cases as false memories and another 23% as having accepted the event to some degree. Where the suggestion carried self-relevant information and an imagination exercise and no photograph, the rate was 46.1%. Their paper calls itself a mega-analysis, on the ground that the data were not amenable to meta-analysis. Andrews and Brewin then obtained Murphy's transcripts and recoded them for six suggested core details. Participants judged to have false memories recalled fewer than two of the six on average. Of those with full false memories, 20% did not explicitly recall being lost, and nor did 58% of those with partial ones. Thirty-eight of the 123 described a relevant past experience that they themselves told apart from the fake one. Their subtractions run in steps: removing 22 participants with potentially true experiences takes 35% to 17%, removing seven with no recall of being lost takes it to 11%, and removing nine who did not self-report a memory takes it to 4%. Wade, Riesthuis, Bücken, Otgaar and Loftus answered that a reconstructive memory should be expected to contain real fragments, and that even low rates matter in legal settings. Murphy and Greene answered that no single coding scheme should decide the question. Brewin and Andrews replied that concerns about the paradigm's reliability, validity and generalisability persist. Szojka, Block and La Rooy, writing against the paradigm's use in court, still put the replication question plainly: asked whether the 1995 result can be replicated, they answer a confident yes, and move their objection to external validity.

study.cite: Murphy, G., Dawson, C. A., Huston, C., Ballantyne, L., Barrett, E., Cowman, C. S., Fitzsimons, C., Maher, J., Ryan, K. M., & Greene, C. M. (2023). Lost in the mall again: a preregistered replication and extension of Loftus & Pickrell (1995). Memory, 31(6), 818-830.

limits: The technique is bounded by plausibility, and the boundary was mapped with the mall event itself. Pezdek, Finger and Hodge had 20 people read a younger sibling or close relative one true event and two false ones, being lost in a mall and receiving an enema. Three false events were remembered and all three were the mall. In their study of children, 19 aged 5 to 7 and 20 aged 9 to 12 heard both false events. Fourteen recalled the mall and not the enema, one the reverse, and three recalled both. Most of the 39 recalled neither. What the paradigm produces is also reversible. Greene, Murphy and colleagues debriefed the 123 replication participants and asked again three days later. Of the 101 who returned, 6 still reported a memory and 8 still reported a belief, down from 13.8% and 52%. Most of the memories that survived were ones the participant no longer believed. That paper's abstract gives the follow-up belief rate as 7% where its results section gives 8%, and the count of eight is used here. Oeberst, Wachendörfer, Imhoff and Blank got a similar reversal on 52 participants, using two negative childhood events nominated by parents rather than the mall event. False memories reached 27% under minimal and 56% under massive suggestion, then fell to 15% and 23% after two sensitisation procedures. A year later, four participants in the massive condition still qualified. Bücken, Riesthuis, Caon, Cucu and Otgaar ran a larger blind implantation with 294 participants and found the opposite for training, with false reports rising rather than falling. That is a different induction method and it is not a test of the mall protocol. Several documents could not be obtained. Murphy and colleagues' replication is paywalled and is described here from its abstract and from the two later papers that use its data; the mock juror finding and the 35% figure are read that way. Crook and Dean's critique, Loftus's reply, their second reply and Coan's account are all in Ethics and Behavior and were not read in full; the dates and pilot counts above come from the PubMed abstract of Crook and Dean. Scoboria and colleagues' mega-analysis was read in abstract. Searches ran across Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, institutional repositories and the open web. This entry does not attempt to settle the recovered-memory dispute, which is the argument the numbers on this page are recruited into.
misreadings: The headline is usually given as a quarter of people being made to remember anything. The event was ordinary, a relative had confirmed it was plausible for that person, it sat among three real memories, and the descriptions ran to a third as many words as the true ones. Loftus and Pickrell were explicit that they were making no claim about what percentage of people can be misled. The rate is also read as a self-report when it is a coder's verdict on a transcript, and the replication shows the two coming apart: 35% coded against 14% who said they remembered. False belief is not false memory either, and the coding schemes separate them, with Scoboria's scheme putting 30.4% as memories and a further 23% as acceptance of some degree. The ethics fight around the study is often collapsed into the science. Crook and Dean argued in Ethics and Behavior that the study has been cited in scholarly and legal arenas to support claims it cannot support. Their abstract also charges methodological errors, thin peer review and supervision, and the announcement of preliminary results four days after approval. Loftus replied in the same issue that their essay misstated her findings and distorted the history of the research, and questioned how it came to be accepted. Both sides are reported here and neither is adjudicated. Finally, the study is treated as settling whether recovered memories of abuse are real. Brewin and Andrews say the field's results get exaggerated in expert witness reports. Wade and colleagues say low rates would still matter in court. Szojka and colleagues say a plausible event embedded in true ones tells you little about allegations of abuse.
